document_check.note: The document is Xia X, Duffner LA, Bintener C, Bradshaw A, Lamirel D, Jönsson L. 'Diagnostic and prognostic multimodal prediction models in Alzheimer's disease: A scoping review', J Alzheimers Dis 2025;108(S1):S209-S221, doi:10.1177/13872877251351630. It includes 138 studies, 89 of which (64.5%) predict MCI progression to AD dementia. This matches the cited sentence.

cited_result: The review's census of included studies: 138 multimodal prediction-model studies across the AD spectrum, the largest share (89; 64.5%) targeting progression from MCI to AD dementia.
tool_reason: The cited result is a synthesis finding (a count and distribution of included studies) from a review with a registered protocol, a systematic multi-database search and PRISMA-ScR reporting. It is closer to a systematic review than to a narrative review, so ROBIS can judge whether study identification and selection bias the census.

domains.rationale: The protocol was registered, and the eligibility criteria are explicit and suited to a map of multimodal prediction models. The English-only and peer-reviewed-only restrictions are noted, but for a descriptive map they are unlikely to bias the relative distribution of objectives much.

signalling.question: 1.1 Did the review adhere to pre-defined objectives and eligibility criteria?
signalling.quote: The literature review protocol was registered with the Open Science Framework (osf.io/zkw6g).

signalling.question: 1.2 Were the eligibility criteria appropriate for the review question?
signalling.quote: (4) the prediction models incorporated two or more data modalities, with studies using only neuroimaging modalities (e.g., MRI and PET) considered single-modality and therefore excluded

signalling.question: 1.3 Were eligibility criteria unambiguous?
signalling.quote: (3) the studies focused on prediction models trained on data from individuals with suspected AD symptoms

signalling.question: 1.4 Were all restrictions in eligibility criteria based on study characteristics appropriate?
signalling.quote: Exclusion criteria for the literature review were: (1) records that were editorials, commentaries, reviews, or viewpoints, (2) studies that did not report model performance measures, and (3) retracted studies.

signalling.question: 1.5 Were any restrictions in eligibility criteria based on sources of information appropriate?
signalling.quote: (5) they were original investigations published in peer-reviewed journals.

domains.rationale: One researcher screened titles and abstracts. Records were ranked by semantic similarity to 111 benchmark papers and read only until they 'no longer appeared to be relevant'; after that, only titles were screened. The search was limited to English. 42 of the 138 included studies (30%) came from reference lists rather than the database search, which shows the search missed many eligible studies, as the authors concede. Both problems bear directly on the completeness of the cited count.

signalling.question: 2.1 Did the search include an appropriate range of databases/electronic sources for published and unpublished reports?
signalling.quote: We conducted a systematic literature search of literature, until January 15, 2024, with no restriction on the inception date, in Medline, Embase, and Web of Science.

signalling.question: 2.2 Were methods additional to database searching used to identify relevant reports?
signalling.quote: In addition, references of included articles were scrutinized for eligible studies.

signalling.question: 2.3 Were the terms and structure of the search strategy likely to retrieve as many eligible studies as possible?
signalling.quote: The remaining 96 studies, along with 42 additional studies identified from their reference lists, were included in the literature review (Figure 1).

signalling.question: 2.4 Were restrictions based on date, publication format or language appropriate?
signalling.quote: We restricted our search to publications in English.

signalling.question: 2.5 Were efforts made to minimise error in selection of studies?
signalling.quote: Then, the researcher reviewed the titles and abstracts by the rank of the similarity measure until the titles and abstracts no longer appeared to be relevant. Lastly, the researcher screened only the titles of the remaining references.

domains.rationale: Extraction was checked by a second reviewer. However, only the best-performing model per study was extracted, and no risk-of-bias or quality appraisal was done. This matters little for the cited count of studies and objectives but matters a great deal for any performance statement.

signalling.question: 3.1 Were efforts made to minimise error in data collection?
signalling.quote: A secondary review of the extracted data was conducted by a different reviewer than the one who initially extracted the data.

signalling.question: 3.2 Were sufficient study characteristics available for both review authors and readers to be able to interpret the results?
signalling.quote: The list of included studies can be found in Supplemental Material 2.

signalling.question: 3.3 Were all relevant study results collected for use in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: It was common for studies to evaluate multiple candidate prediction models, in which case we extracted data from the prediction models with the best performance based on area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) or accuracy if AUC was not reported.

signalling.question: 3.4 Was risk of bias (or methodological quality) formally assessed using appropriate criteria?
signalling.quote: Firstly, the studies included in the literature review did not go through quality assessments.

signalling.question: 3.5 Were efforts made to minimise error in risk of bias assessment?
signalling.quote: Since no systematic quality assessment was performed on the studies included in this literature review, the information should not be interpreted as representing the best prediction models for decision-making support.

domains.rationale: A narrative charting of all included studies by objective suits the cited descriptive finding. However, no sensitivity or robustness analysis was done, and the report is internally inconsistent: 14 (10.1%) externally validated studies in the text against 13 (9.4%) in Table 1. Primary-study biases were not assessed; only a subset of models was excluded from the 'well-performing' summary.

signalling.question: 4.1 Did the synthesis include all studies that it should?
signalling.quote: The data from the prediction models in the included studies were synthesized narratively and charted based on the outcomes the studies aimed to predict.

signalling.question: 4.2 Were all pre-defined analyses reported or departures explained?
signalling.quote: I searched for a statement of deviations from the registered OSF protocol and found none. The protocol content is not reproduced in the document.

signalling.question: 4.3 Was the synthesis appropriate given the nature and similarity in the research questions, study designs and outcomes across included studies?
signalling.quote: Notably, a single study may have multiple predictive objectives, such as distinguishing AD from Lewy body dementia and differentiating AD from vascular dementia, each of which was treated as a separate prediction model.

signalling.question: 4.4 Was between-study variation (heterogeneity) minimal or addressed in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: For prognostic models, such as those predicting future progression from MCI to AD dementia, the prediction horizon varied across studies, with two to four years being the most common.

signalling.question: 4.5 Were the findings robust, e.g. as demonstrated through sensitivity analyses?
signalling.quote: Only 14 (10.1%) studies conducted external validation for the prediction models.

signalling.question: 4.6 Were biases in primary studies minimal or addressed in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: For this summary, we excluded prediction models that did not report basic demographic information, were trained on less than 100 persons, or included tests that were key criteria for defining the outcome as predictors

domains.domain: Phase 3. Risk of bias in the review
domains.rationale: The authors acknowledge that the search missed studies and that no quality assessment was done. They do not discuss single-reviewer, similarity-truncated screening, which is the main threat to the completeness of the census. They consider relevance appropriately and do not rely on statistical significance.

signalling.question: A. Did the interpretation of findings address all of the concerns identified in Domains 1 to 4?
signalling.quote: Thirdly, our search missed some studies that did not include clear terminology that indicated the multiple data modalities in their models.

signalling.question: B. Was the relevance of identified studies to the review's research question appropriately considered?
signalling.quote: Predicting the future progression from MCI to AD dementia was the most common objective of prediction models for AD.

signalling.question: C. Did the reviewers avoid emphasising results on the basis of their statistical significance?
signalling.quote: Instead, it can serve as a reference for future model development.

overall: High risk of bias in the review
overall_rationale: The cited result is a census (138 studies, 64.5% on MCI-to-AD). Its completeness depends on study identification and selection, which carries high concern. Title and abstract screening was done by one reviewer and cut off by a semantic-similarity ranking, the remainder was screened on titles only, and the search was English-only. Nearly a third of the included studies came from reference lists, not from the database search. No quality appraisal was done, and the interpretation does not address the screening method. The relative share of MCI-to-AD studies is probably less affected than the absolute count.

applicability.domain: Relevance to the citing review's question
applicability.rationale: The review maps multimodal prediction models across the AD spectrum, and the cited statement is only about what that literature contains.
